en opvækst.explanation: "En opvækst" means "an upbringing". It comes from the verb "at vokse op" (to grow up). To say where you grew up, put "i" (in) and the place after it: "en opvækst i Jylland" (an upbringing in Jutland).

related.en: an upbringing in manners and behavior

en ordbog.explanation: "En ordbog" means "a dictionary". It is built from "ord" (word) and "bog" (book). The same "ord" is in "et ordsprog" (a proverb).

en ordliste.explanation: "En ordliste" means "a word list / glossary". It is built from "ord" (word) and "en liste" (a list). Do not mix it up with "en ordbog" (a dictionary), which is a book that explains words: "Jeg slår ordet op i en ordbog" (I look the word up in a dictionary).

en ordning.explanation: "En ordning" means "an arrangement / scheme". It comes from the verb "at ordne" (to put in order). To talk about a pension scheme, add "pension" in front: "en pensionsordning" (a pension scheme).

en ordre.explanation: "En ordre" means "an order (command)". To talk about goods a customer asks a company to supply, use it too: "en ordre på ti stole" (an order for ten chairs). To order food in a restaurant, use "at bestille" (to order) instead: "Jeg vil gerne bestille en pizza" (I would like to order a pizza).

en organisation.explanation: "En organisation" means "an organization". It is the noun for the verb "at organisere" (to organize). To talk about how work is arranged, use it too: "organisationen af arbejdet" (the organization of the work).

en orkan.explanation: "En orkan" means "a hurricane". In Danish weather reports, "orkan" is the strongest level on the wind scale.

en orm.explanation: "En orm" means "a worm". It is the end of "en regnorm" (an earthworm), built from "regn" (rain) and "orm".

en ostehandler.explanation: "En ostehandler" means "a cheesemonger". The ending "-handler" is also in "en fiskehandler" (a fishmonger).

en ostemad.explanation: "En ostemad" means "a cheese sandwich". It is built from "ost" (cheese) and "en mad" (a sandwich). Without an article, "mad" means food in general: "Vi laver mad" (We are cooking).

en osteskærer.explanation: "En osteskærer" means "a cheese slicer". It is built from "ost" (cheese) and the verb "at skære" (to cut). The same ending is in "en pizzaskærer" (a pizza cutter).

en overbetjent.explanation: "En overbetjent" means "a police sergeant". It is built from "over-" (higher) and "en betjent" (an officer). The same "over-" is in "en overlæge" (a senior doctor).

en overbevisning.explanation: "En overbevisning" means "a conviction", as in a firm belief. It comes from the verb "at overbevise" (to convince). For a court's guilty verdict, use "en domfældelse" instead: "Efter domfældelsen kom han i fængsel" (After the conviction, he went to prison).

en overdosis.explanation: "En overdosis" means "an overdose". It is built from "over-" (over) and "en dosis" (a dose). To say what someone died from, use "af" (of): "Han døde af en overdosis" (He died of an overdose).

en overenskomst.explanation: "En overenskomst" means "a collective agreement". Many jobs in Denmark are covered by one. To ask whether a workplace has one, say: "Har I overenskomst?" (Do you have a collective agreement?)

en overflade.explanation: "En overflade" means "a surface". It is built from "over" (over) and "en flade" (a flat area). To say something is on it, use "på" (on): "på overfladen" (on the surface).

en overførsel.explanation: "En overførsel" means "a transfer". It is the noun for the verb "at overføre" (to transfer). To talk about a payment between bank accounts, add "bank" in front: "en bankoverførsel" (a bank transfer). To talk about moving computer files, say: "overførsel af filer" (transfer of files).

en overgang.explanation: "En overgang" means "a transition". It comes from "at gå over" (to go across). To talk about a place where people cross a street, say: "en fodgængerovergang" (a pedestrian crossing).

en overnatning.explanation: "En overnatning" means "an overnight stay". To ask for a stay that includes breakfast, say: "overnatning med morgenmad" (a stay with breakfast).

en overraskelse.explanation: "En overraskelse" means "a surprise". It comes from the verb "at overraske" (to surprise). To tell someone you have a surprise for them, say: "Jeg har en overraskelse til dig" (I have a surprise for you).

en oversigt.explanation: "En oversigt" means "an overview". It is built from "over" (over) and "sigt" (sight), the same "sigt" as in "en udsigt" (a view).

en overskrift.explanation: "En overskrift" means "a headline". It is built from "over" (over) and "skrift" (writing), so it is the writing that stands above a text.

en oversvømmelse.explanation: "En oversvømmelse" means "a flood". It comes from the verb "at oversvømme" (to flood). To warn that water may rise, say: "Der er risiko for oversvømmelse" (There is a risk of flooding).

en oversættelse.explanation: "En oversættelse" means "a translation". It comes from the verb "at oversætte" (to translate). For someone who translates spoken words, use "en tolk" (an interpreter) instead: "Vi fik en tolk til mødet" (We got an interpreter for the meeting).

en oversætter.explanation: "En oversætter" means "a translator". It is the person who does "at oversætte" (to translate). For someone who translates spoken words, use "en tolk" (an interpreter) instead: "Jeg bruger en tolk til mødet" (I am using an interpreter for the meeting).

en overvejelse.explanation: "En overvejelse" means "a consideration". It is the noun for the verb "at overveje" (to consider). To say something happened after some thought, use the plural: "efter nogle overvejelser" (after some consideration).

en ovn.explanation: "En ovn" means "an oven". To say you turn it on, use "at tænde" (to turn on): "Jeg tænder ovnen" (I turn on the oven). For the cooking surface on top, use "en kogeplade" (a stovetop) instead: "Jeg koger vand på kogepladen" (I boil water on the stovetop).

et offentligt rum.explanation: "Et offentligt rum" means "a public space". After "i det" (in the), the adjective ends in "-e": "i det offentlige rum" (in public space). The word "et rum" can also mean "a room": "Lejligheden har tre rum" (The apartment has three rooms).

et offentligt toilet.explanation: "Et offentligt toilet" means "a public restroom". The adjective ends in "-t" here, but it ends in "-e" after "det" (the): "det offentlige toilet" (the public restroom).

et offer.explanation: "Et offer" means "a victim". To talk about someone hurt in a crime, say: "Politiet talte med offeret" (The police spoke with the victim). It also means "a sacrifice". To say something costs you something you give up, say: "Det kræver et offer" (It takes a sacrifice).

et omdømme.explanation: "Et omdømme" means "a reputation". It is built from "om" (around) and "at dømme" (to judge). To say something harms it, use "at skade" (to damage): "Skandalen skadede firmaets omdømme" (The scandal damaged the company's reputation).

et omklædningsrum.explanation: "Et omklædningsrum" means "a locker room". It is built from "omklædning" (changing clothes) and "et rum" (a room).

et område.explanation: "Et område" means "an area". When you talk about a subject someone knows well, it means "a field": "Hun er ekspert på dette område" (She is an expert in this field).

et ophold.explanation: "Et ophold" means "a stay". It comes from the verb "at opholde sig" (to stay somewhere). It is also in "en opholdstilladelse" (a residence permit).

et opholdsrum.explanation: "Et opholdsrum" means "a lounge". It is built from "et ophold" (a stay) and "et rum" (a room). Do not mix it up with "en stue" (a living room), which is in a home: "Vi sidder i stuen" (We are sitting in the living room).

et opkald.explanation: "Et opkald" means "a phone call". When you mean the talk itself, use "en samtale" (a conversation): "Vi havde en lang samtale" (We had a long conversation). To name a call nobody picked up, say: "et ubesvaret opkald" (an unanswered call).

et opkøb.explanation: "Et opkøb" means "an acquisition / buyout". It comes from "at købe op" (to buy up). To talk about a takeover the owners did not want, say: "et fjendtligt opkøb" (a hostile takeover).

et oplæg.explanation: "Et oplæg" means "a presentation / proposal". To say someone gives a talk, use "at holde" (to hold): "Han holder et oplæg om klima" (He gives a presentation about climate).

et oprør.explanation: "Et oprør" means "a rebellion / uprising". To say someone refuses to obey, use "at gøre oprør mod" (to rebel against): "Børnene gjorde oprør mod reglerne" (The children rebelled against the rules).

et opslag.explanation: "Et opslag" means "a post", as on social media: "Hun skrev et opslag om sin ferie" (She wrote a post about her vacation). To talk about a paper notice on a wall, use it too: "Der hænger et opslag på skolen" (There is a notice up at the school).

et optog.explanation: "Et optog" means "a parade". To say people march together in one, use "at gå i optog" (to walk in a parade): "Børnene går i optog" (The children march in a parade).

et ord.explanation: "Et ord" means "a word". It is the start of compounds such as "en ordbog" (a dictionary, literally a word book). To say you keep a promise, use "at holde" (to keep): "Jeg holder mit ord" (I keep my word).

et ordforråd.explanation: "Et ordforråd" means "a vocabulary". It is built from "ord" (word) and "et forråd" (a stock of supplies), so it is literally a stock of words. To say someone knows many words, say: "Hun har et stort ordforråd" (She has a large vocabulary).

et ordspil.explanation: "Et ordspil" means "a pun / wordplay". It is built from "et ord" (a word) and "et spil" (a game), so it is literally a word game. To say you made one, say: "Jeg lavede et ordspil" (I made a pun).

et ordsprog.explanation: "Et ordsprog" means "a proverb". To give a well-known Danish one: "Den, der intet vover, intet vinder" (Nothing ventured, nothing gained).

et organ.explanation: "Et organ" means "an organ", as in a part of the body. To talk about an authority, it also means "a body": "et offentligt organ" (a public body).

et overblik.explanation: "Et overblik" means "an overview". It is built from "over" (over) and "et blik" (a look). To say you have lost your grip on things, say: "Jeg har mistet overblikket" (I have lost track of things).

et overfald.explanation: "Et overfald" means "an assault". It comes from the verb "at overfalde" (to attack). If the attacker also steals something, use "et røveri" (a robbery) instead: "Der var et røveri i banken" (There was a robbery at the bank).

et overskud.explanation: "Et overskud" means "a surplus". In a company's accounts, it means the profit left after costs: "Regnskabet viser et overskud på en million" (The accounts show a surplus of one million). To say you have energy to spare, use "at have overskud" (to have energy to spare): "Jeg har ikke overskud i dag" (I do not have the energy today).

et overskæg.explanation: "Et overskæg" means "a mustache". It is built from "over" (over) and "et skæg" (a beard), so it is the beard hair above the mouth.

objektiv.explanation: "Objektiv" means "objective". Before an "et" word it ends in "-t": "et objektivt billede" (an objective picture). To talk about a camera lens, use the noun "et objektiv" (a lens): "Han skiftede objektiv" (He changed the lens).

obligatorisk.explanation: "Obligatorisk" means "mandatory". To say who it applies to, put "for" (for) after it: "Kurset er obligatorisk for alle" (The course is mandatory for everyone).

odds.explanation: "Odds" means "odds". To say you bet on something, use "at satse på" (to bet on): "Jeg satser på det røde hold" (I am betting on the red team).

offentlig.explanation: "Offentlig" means "public". To talk about transport everyone can use, say: "offentlig transport" (public transport). The opposite is "privat" (private): "en privat skole" (a private school).

offentlighed.explanation: "Offentlighed" means "the public". It is built from the adjective "offentlig" (public). To say who the police asked for help, say: "Politiet bad offentligheden om hjælp" (The police asked the public for help).

offentligt.explanation: "Offentligt" means "publicly". It comes from "offentlig" (public). To say someone speaks in front of everyone, say: "Han talte offentligt om sygdommen" (He spoke publicly about the illness).

officiel.explanation: "Officiel" means "official". Do not mix it up with "offentlig" (public), which is about things that belong to everyone: "et offentligt bibliotek" (a public library).

officielt.explanation: "Officielt" means "officially". It comes from "officiel" (official). To say what the rules say, whatever people do, say: "Officielt er det forbudt, men alle gør det" (Officially it is forbidden, but everyone does it).

offline.explanation: "Offline" means "offline". To say you disconnect from the web, use "at gå offline" (to go offline): "Jeg går offline nu" (I am going offline now).

oftest.explanation: "Oftest" means "most often". It is the last step of "ofte" (often): "ofte", "oftere" (more often), "oftest". To say what you eat most often, say: "Jeg spiser oftest ris" (I most often eat rice).

og.explanation: "Og" means "and". It is said without the "g" sound. Do not mix it up with "også" (also, too): "Jeg kan også lide te" (I also like tea).

også.explanation: "Også" means "too". In a negative sentence, use "heller ikke" (either) instead: "Jeg kommer heller ikke" (I am not coming either). Do not mix it up with "og" (and): "te og kaffe" (tea and coffee).

okay.explanation: "Okay" means "okay". To agree to a plan, answer with it: "Skal vi tage bussen?" "Okay." (Shall we take the bus? Okay.)

oksekød.explanation: "Oksekød" means "beef". It is built from "en okse" (an ox) and "kød" (meat), so it is literally ox meat.

oktober.explanation: "Oktober" means "October". Danish spells it with a "k", where English has a "c".

oldnordisk.explanation: "Oldnordisk" means "Old Norse". The "old-" means ancient, as in "oldtiden" (ancient times). To say you study it, use "at læse" (to study): "Han læser oldnordisk" (He studies Old Norse).

olivenolie.explanation: "Olivenolie" means "olive oil". It is built from "en oliven" (an olive) and "olie" (oil).

om.explanation: "Om" means "about". To say what a book is about, use it: "en bog om Danmark" (a book about Denmark). It also means "in" for time from now: "om en uge" (a week from now). It also means "whether", after a verb like "at vide" (to know): "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer" (I do not know whether he is coming). To say how long something lasts, use "i" (for) instead: "i en uge" (for a week).

om lidt.explanation: "Om lidt" means "in a little while". To promise that you will arrive soon, say: "Jeg kommer om lidt" (I am coming in a little while). The "om" in it is the same "om" as in "om en uge" (a week from now).

om ugen.explanation: "Om ugen" means "per week". The same pattern works for a day: "to gange om dagen" (twice a day).

om året.explanation: "Om året" means "a year", for how often something happens. The same pattern works for a month: "en gang om måneden" (once a month).

ombord.explanation: "Ombord" means "on board". To say someone steps onto a ferry, use it with "på" (on): "Hun går ombord på færgen" (She goes on board the ferry). The opposite is "i land" (ashore): "Vi går i land" (We go ashore).

omfattende.explanation: "Omfattende" means "extensive". To say damage is extensive, say: "Skaden er omfattende" (The damage is extensive). To talk about the size of a house, use "stor" (big) instead: "et stort hus" (a big house).

omgivet.explanation: "Omgivet" means "surrounded". It comes from the verb "at omgive" (to surround). To say what surrounds a house, use "af" (by): "Huset er omgivet af en have" (The house is surrounded by a garden).

omgående.explanation: "Omgående" means "immediately". To ask someone to act at once, say: "Kontakt os omgående" (Contact us immediately).

omhyggelig.explanation: "Omhyggelig" means "careful", as in thorough. To describe how a plan was made, say: "en omhyggelig planlægning" (careful planning). To tell someone to avoid danger, use "forsigtig" (cautious) instead: "Vær forsigtig!" (Be careful!)

omkring.explanation: "Omkring" means "around". To say where something is, use it for a place: "omkring hjørnet" (around the corner). To give a rough amount, use it for "about": "omkring hundrede mennesker" (about a hundred people). To give a rough time, use it before the clock: "omkring klokken tre" (around three o'clock).

omsider.explanation: "Omsider" means "at last". To say a long job is finally done, say: "Nu er hun omsider færdig" (Now she is at last finished).

omsorg.explanation: "En omsorg" means "care". To say who receives it, use "for" (for): "omsorg for børn" (care for children).

omsorgsfuld.explanation: "Omsorgsfuld" means "caring". It is built from "omsorg" (care) and "-fuld" (full of), the same ending as in "smertefuld" (painful). To describe a teacher, say: "en omsorgsfuld lærer" (a caring teacher).

omstændelig.explanation: "Omstændelig" means "long-winded". To describe a task with too many steps, say: "en omstændelig procedure" (a long-winded procedure). Do not mix it up with "kompliceret" (complicated), which is hard to understand: "Det er et kompliceret problem" (It is a complicated problem).

omtrent.explanation: "Omtrent" means "about". To give a rough number, use it before the number: "omtrent tyve mennesker" (about twenty people). To say something is nearly done, it also means "more or less": "Det er omtrent færdigt" (It is more or less done).

omvendt.explanation: "Omvendt" means "reverse". To say a book is the wrong way around, say: "Bogen står omvendt på hylden" (The book is the wrong way around on the shelf). At the start of a sentence, it means "conversely": "Han er høj. Omvendt er hun lille" (He is tall. Conversely, she is short).

ond.explanation: "Ond" means "evil". It also means "painful" in set phrases, where it ends in "-t". To say something hurts, say: "Det gør ondt" (It hurts).

ondskab.explanation: "Ondskab" means "malice". It is built from "ond" (evil) and "-skab", the same ending as in "venskab" (friendship).

ondt.explanation: "Ondt" means "hurt". To say a body part hurts, use "at have" (to have) with "ondt" and "i" (in): "Jeg har ondt i ryggen" (My back hurts), literally "I have pain in the back". To say something hurts, use "at gøre" (to do): "Det gør ondt" (It hurts).

online.explanation: "Online" means "online". It keeps the same ending before an "en" word and an "et" word: "en online butik" (an online store), "et online kursus" (an online course). To say you shop on the web, use "at handle" (to shop): "Jeg handler online" (I shop online).

onsdag.explanation: "Onsdag" means "Wednesday". To say something happens next Wednesday, say: "Vi ses på onsdag" (We will see each other on Wednesday). To say it happens every Wednesday, say: "Jeg træner om onsdagen" (I work out on Wednesdays).

op.explanation: "Op" means "up". To tell someone to move upward, say: "Kom op!" (Come up!) To say where someone already is, use "oppe" (up there) instead: "Han er oppe på loftet" (He is up in the attic). It is also part of "at stå op" (to get up out of bed): "Jeg står op klokken seks" (I get up at six).

opad.explanation: "Opad" means "upward". The ending "-ad" names a direction, as in "udad" (outward).

opbakning.explanation: "Opbakning" means "support". It is the noun for "at bakke op" (to back up). To name what receives the support, use "til" (for): "opbakning til forslaget" (support for the proposal).

opdateret.explanation: "Opdateret" means "updated". It is the "-et" form of the verb "at opdatere" (to update). To say someone knows the latest news, use it for the person: "Er du opdateret på nyhederne?" (Are you up to date on the news?)

opdraget.explanation: "Opdraget" means "brought up". With "godt" (well) it describes someone polite: "Han er godt opdraget" (He is well brought up). With "dårligt" (badly) it describes someone rude: "Drengen er dårligt opdraget" (The boy is badly brought up).

opfindsom.explanation: "Opfindsom" means "inventive". It is built from the verb "at opfinde" (to invent) and "-som", the same ending as in "hjælpsom" (helpful). To describe a solution, say: "en opfindsom løsning" (an inventive solution).
